newsitem.title: INDIA: Investor caution seen limiting India stocks rally.
newsitem.headline: Investor caution seen limiting India stocks rally.

text.p: Jittery investors are likely to put the brakes on a boom in Indian blue chips this week, but underlying sentiment is still bullish, dealers and analysts said at the weekend.
"There is cautious optimism...the rally has lasted for a long time," Gul Teckchandani, chief investment officer at Sun Foreign & Colonial Asset Management, told Reuters.
Dealers said liquidity was improving as retail investors, long equity-shy, were making commitments to pick up small capitalisation stocks.
"They (small investors) have started their purchases, but have yet to gather a critical mass," said the research head of a local brokerage.
However, Teckchandani added: "The mood is definitely more optimistic...nobody wants to miss the bus."
The Bombay Stock Exchange's (BSE) top 30-share index rallied 154.26 points or 4.7 percent to end at 3,418.32 in the week to Friday -- up nearly 11 percent since the close of 1996.

Participants said a flurry of buy orders by foreign funds combined with increased speculative bidding drove up the market last week. They said funds were looking at defensive bets in the consumer non-durables, pharmaceutical and service industries.
"People are going in for defensive...recession-proof stocks," Teckchandani said.
Sanjay Agarwal, chief executive at Lloyds Securities, said he was advising his clients to accumulate good quality stocks at every decline. "Be cautious and keep buying at lower levels.
"Good stocks are showing signs of moving up...there is strength in the market," he said.
The trend of select pivotal counters like BHEL, Infosys Technologies and Cadbury India climbing to 52-week highs was a good sign, dealers said.
Indian shares have been helped by Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's promise to pep up industrial growth and announce measures to revive stock markets.
Last week Deve Gowda reiterated his resolve to attract $10 billion in foreign investment annually and promised a set of decisions to boost foreign investment.
"Currently, it is only talking. Let's see some action," said Colonial's Teckchandani.
Net foreign portfolio investment in India was $2.0 billion in 1995/96 (April-March). Foreign direct investment (FDI) was $2.13 billion.
Some traders hope the government will give excise relief to industries like cement, steel and consumer goods that are hit by a slowdown in demand and a squeeze on margins.

Market expectations include the exemption of dividends from taxes, the scrapping of a controversial minimum alternate tax imposed in last July's budget and allowing companies to buy back their shares.
Since hitting a three-year low of 2,713.12 on December 4, the Bombay index is up 705.20 points or nearly 26 percent.
